description.narrative:
At the beginning of the previous grant period, the WE-Care team completed the endline evaluation of Phase IV spanning the period from April 2020 to August 2023. The key successes highlighted in the Phase IV evaluation validates what was noted in the previous grant proposal and are summarized below: • Awareness building and capacity strengthening trainings have led to effective stakeholder engagement, buy-in and ownership of the program which has resulted in kick-starting policy-making processes to address UCDW, with Oxfamand partners being recognized as key technical expert organizations. These efforts are continuing to show results in Phase V. With the support of Oxfam in Kenya, the Kenyan government launched the Time Use Survey, their first statistical product in October 2023 and is in the process of developing their National Care Policy inviting Oxfam to be on the Technical Working Group. In Zimbabwe, the Ministry of Women’s Affairs, Small and Medium Enterprises has prioritized the Care Agenda and has asked for collaboration with Oxfamand its partners on developing a national care policy. Teams in Uganda and Zimbabwe are developing care policy scorecards at the national level; and, at the regional level, Africa Leadership Foundation (ALF) and some selected women’s Rights Organizations (WROs) participated in the validation of a position paper on positive masculinity organized by the African Union Commission Women, Gender and Youth Directorate (AUC-WGYD), capturing how UCDW drives violence against women gender-based violence (GBV). • Project efforts led to public opinions and narratives shifting to acknowledge UCDW as a critical barrier to gender equality and women’s economic justice. At the community level, men have started contributing to household chores and taking care of children. This was done through awareness creation, training, and capacity building, engaging media, academia, local community champions, government departments, parliamentarians, and other influencers. These efforts are continuing in Phase V, for instance, Youth Alive Kenya (YAK) has designed community forums to involve male champions and influential leaders in open discussions to address UCDW. The Network of Ethiopian Women's Associations (NEWA) in Ethiopia has forged partnership with a media house to enhance their capacities to advocate for issues of UCDW. • Several WROs, civil society organizations (CSOs), youth groups, community-based organizations (CBOs) are also now undertaking activities and engaging in policy discussions on UCDW as a result of peer-to-peer engagement by partners and Oxfam. For example, the evaluation revealed 81 organizations in Zimbabwe are now working towards addressing UCDW as compared to 6 at the start of the project,and Uganda Women’s Network's (UWONET) outreach to grassroots organizations (Uganda and Gals Forum International (GAFI)) led to the creation of Women’s Caucuses by elected women councillors who have now become care champions and advocates. Movement building and peer-to-peer learning on UCDW will continue in the next phase. UWONET is also drafting an unpaid care policy that WROs/civil society and other actors can adapt and institutionalize within their organizations. • At the regional level, the program continues to make cross-thematic linkages between the WE-Care Program and other Oxfam program areas, for example, Oxfam’s participation in Oxfam in Africa’s (OiA) COP-28 convening and the development and submission of a position paper on UCDW and Climate Change in that space.
Oxfam and partners continue to reflect on the challenges and lessons from the last phase of the program and how to incorporate it in the ongoing Phase V. • Oxfam and partners recognize that fostering healthy engagement with decision-makers – political leaders, religiousand traditional leaders, and policy makers – has potential to contribute to the adoption and implementation of policies and instruments for tackling gender equality and UCDW. This was highlighted in the Phase IV evaluation and the ongoing Phase V builds on this reflection. For example, in Uganda, UWONET has designed training sessions which has led to action plans developed by the participantsto integrate the 5Rs framework and human rights-based approaches into religious and cultural teachings. • The work on shifting narratives, especially on patriarchal norms and practices such as gender bias, negative social norms and attitudes, and the influences of culture and religion remains crucial. In Phase V, partners have found varied ways to engage with men champions. For instance, Youth Alive Kenya (YAK) is holding men engagement forums, building the capacity of male change champions on UCDW. At the regional level,the Africa Leadership Foundation (ALF) in partnership with Oxfam in Africa (OiA) organized two virtual dialogues with youths from Sub-Saharan Africa convening 87 Africans (49 women and 38 men) from 21 African Member States. This led to the creation of the AfricanYouth Network of UCDW Advocates (AYNUA), coordinated by ALF and OiA in collaboration with AU Women Gender and Youth Directorate (WGYD) and other critical stakeholders. • Finally, the Phase IV evaluation noted the need for investing in organizational capacities ofpartners and Oxfam offices in the program countries to improve program effectiveness and foster sustainable change. During Phase V there is an intentional effort to identify the capacity needs in terms of skill development and organizational development. Several technical trainings are underway for Partners and Oxfam teams in areas where they have expressed needs e.g. advocacy, communications, monitoring and evaluation etc. In addition, organizational needs have been identified by partners for support in the coming two years.

participating-org.narrative:
Uganda Women#s Network (UWONET) was formed in 1993 as an advocacy network by Ugandan Women; 16 national women#s organisations, institutions and 9 individuals to steer women#s rights, gender transformation and equality agenda. The network was formed out of the East African Preparatory Conference held in Kampala in 1993 to spearhead Uganda women#s efforts which led to the participation in the UN World Conference on Women held in Beijing in 1995. UWONET was formed to champion a untied voice and create space for women to collectively address and take action on gender based discrimination in spheres of social economic and political life of women in Ugandaat all levels. UWONET#s core mandate is policy advocacy, however for the past five years it has concentrated programmatically on specific thematic areas and focus i.e. Women#s Leadership and Democratic Governance, Women#s Rights and Access to Justice, Women#s Economic Justice and Empowerment and Institutional Development and Organisational Strengthening. 1. ACHIEVEMENTS What have been the principal results in the past three years that contribute to significant, structural, sustained and positive improvement in the lives of men, women, girls and boys suffering from poverty, injustice, insecurity and exclusion? 1. Reduced tolerance and vulnerability to Gender Based Violence and most especially Violence against Women and Girls as a result of a holistic approach to GBV service delivery. 2. Policy influencing at National, regional and International levels such as engendering the NDP II, pushing for the enactment ofgender bills, policies and laws such as the Land Amendment Act, the Gender Policy, and the Marriage Bill, 2017. UWONET has also utilised global and regional processes and mechanisms to follow up on Uganda#s commitment to fulfilling gender through the CEDAW reporting and UPRM processes. 3. Increased and Improved access to justice and GBV case management as a result of strengthened individual, collective and systematic capacity of human rights and JLOS institutions such as the Police. SGBV desks have been introduced within the Police structure. 4. Increased women#s voice and influence in democratic governance and processes as a result of women#s participation in taking up leadership positions at all levels. Enhanced capacity and voice among district based women#s organisations henceengaged in demanding for accountability for gender equality.3. INSTITUTIONAL PURPOSE Mission: To coordinate action among UWONET membership and targeted stakeholders through networking, capacity building, resource mobilisation, policy research and advocacy for the attainment of gender equality in Uganda.
Institutional objectives: 1) To promote women#s access to power and decision making positions in all sectorsand at all levels. 2) To improve the socio-economic conditions of women and other marginalized groups 3) To work towards the achievement of equal opportunities and rights to women in all sectors and increased access to and control of resources and benefits 4) To work towards the elimination of defilement, rape, violence against women and other forms of abuse against womenand children in society 5) To collect and disseminate information on the priority issues of concern to women. Fields of activity: Key thematic areas are: Women's Leadership and Democratic Governance; Women's Rights and Access to Justice; Women's Economic Justiceand Empowerment and institutional development and Organisation strengthening.
The Geographical areas in which the organization works are Northern, Eastern, Western, West Nile and Karamoja Regions in districts of Lamwo, Kitgum, Agago, Pader, Amuru, Namutumba, Kamuli, Jinja, Buyende, Iganga, Mayuge, Kaliro, Bugiri, Moroto Kotido, Nakapiripirit, Abim, Kaboong, Amudat, Nebbi, Zombo and Mubende among others.
Social Actors are, Women, Girls, district local governments, women councillors, police, health workers, women in business, CBOs, Women groups, Local councils among others.
4. STRATEGIC POSITIONING UWONET operatesin an environment in which there are a number of legal, policies and institutional frameworks for promotion of gender equality and increase in the number of women in politics such as the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda, National Gender Policy 2007, and affirmative Action. However, the rights of women are continually violated and discrimination of women continues.
social Actiors are: Women, Girls, district local governments, women councillors, police, health workers, women councillors, women inbusiness, CBOs, women groups, members of parliament, ministries such as Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development, Ministry of Trade, Ministry of Justice and Contitutional Affairs, Ministry of Education, Ministry of Health among others.
The uniqueness is around policy advocacy and influencing at different levelsi.e. national, regional and international with views from the local levels. In addition, available structures at the local/district levels to reach out to the communities i.e. district women networks.
